sections.overview: This large saturniid moth is native to Madagascar and the Comoros, where it occupies several climate and forest regions.
sections.identification: Adults have broad, scalloped wings in tones ranging from pale ochre to deep brown, with a small translucent-looking spot on each forewing and a much larger ringed eyespot on each hindwing. Eastern Madagascar specimens of the typical form average about 105 mm in wingspan; the Comorian subspecies Antherina suraka comorana is larger at about 125–130 mm and has paler, more ochre forewings. Males tend to have more falcate forewing tips and longer comb-like antenna branches, while females have shorter antennal branches; the available sources do not provide a reliable sex-specific body length, body width, height, or mass.
sections.habitat: On Madagascar it occurs across humid, subhumid, dry, and subarid regions, from near sea level to about 1,900 m elevation. Typical populations favor humid evergreen forests; smaller western forms occur in dry deciduous forest, and the Comorian subspecies also inhabits degraded woodland and urban trees.
sections.diet: The caterpillar is strongly polyphagous: field observations and rearing records list host plants from 23 families. Examples include Maesa, Strophanthus, Eugenia, Schinus, oleander, grapevine, and several fruit trees, so it is not tied to a single tree species.
sections.behavior: Males are attracted to light, but the hour at which they arrive varies by region: one field study caught western males mostly around 10–11 at night and eastern or central males around midnight to 1 after midnight. These are local light-trap observations, not a fixed schedule for every individual.
sections.reproduction: The caterpillar spins a yellowish, net-like cocoon with two layers, within which the pupa develops.
sections.ecology: The Comorian population is treated as the subspecies Antherina suraka comorana, while the smaller western “australis” form is not formally recognized as a separate species. A 2016 barcode study found regional lineages but judged the evidence insufficient to split them into species.
sections.conservation: Researchers document forest loss across parts of its range and argue that habitat protection matters for preserving regional diversity.
